body: Recall that Bitcoin moved higher with stocks on Wednesday, pushing back above $79,146 and into the old swing area that extends to $81,930. The move gave buyers a shot at taking back more control. To do that, they needed to get through the top of the area and stay above it. The rally stalled within the zone, and the price has since fallen back below $79,146. With the Nasdaq and chip stocks under pressure, Bitcoin has given back the rebound and moved back below its 100-day moving average at $76,950. The price was near $76,600 in the chart snapshot after testing the upper edge of the $74,925–$76,052 swing area. The 38.2% retracement of the summer rally comes in at $76,052, making that level the first downside barometer. For sellers, the 100-day MA at $76,950 is the close risk level. Stay below it, and the sellers keep the short-term advantage. Get below $76,052 and stay below, and the focus shifts to the swing-area floor at $74,925. A sustained break of that floor would open the door toward the 200-day MA at $73,195 and then the 50% retracement at $72,554. For buyers, the first job is to hold the swing area and get back above $76,950. If they can get above that moving average and stay above it, the 100- and 200-hour MAs at $78,152 and $78,373 are the next targets. Above those, $79,146 comes back into focus. In the video above, I talk about the technicals in more detail and explain the bias, the risks and targets. A swing area gives traders a range where price has repeatedly changed direction. Here, $76,052 is the first level buyers can lean against, while $74,925 is the floor that defines the broader support area. If price breaks below $76,052 and quickly gets back above it, sellers who chased the break may have to cover. Getting above the 100 day MA would be a risk and bias defining confirmation level that if broken, would give buyers more confidence. If price stays below $76,052, the lower end of the range becomes the next test. That distinction lets traders define their risk before they enter and judge the trade by what price does at the level. title: Oil Rebounds Toward $100 as Democrats’ Sweep Rattles Energy Stocks
summary: Oil prices reversed their recent downtrend on Thursday, a day after Democrats swept control of both the House and Senate, creating a potential legislative check on U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration. Brent crude was up 4.0% to trade at $98.38 per barrel at 3:15 pm ET, while WTI gained 2.9% to $90.65, with prices rising for the first time in four sessions after plunging to a near two-month low on Wednesday. body: Alex Kimani is a veteran finance writer, investor, engineer and researcher for Safehaven.com. Oil prices reversed their recent downtrend on Thursday, a day after Democrats swept control of both the House and Senate, creating a potential legislative check on U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration. Brent crude was up 4.0% to trade at $98.38 per barrel at 3:15 pm ET, while WTI gained 2.9% to $90.65, with prices rising for the first time in four sessions after plunging to a near two-month low on Wednesday. U.S. natural gas prices were flat at $2.95/MMBtu, while European gas prices rebounded 1.9% to €89.72/MWh. The U.S. stock market resumed its recent downtrend on Thursday, with the S&P 500 down more than 3% and the Nasdaq off about 5% in afternoon trading as a selloff in AI chip stocks deepened. AI stocks tied to Texas data centers were hit hard after Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated long-serving Texas governor Greg Abbott, with CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV) falling 7% and Nebius Group (NASDAQ:NBIS) and Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) each sliding 4% in overnight trading on Wednesday. Hinojosa has called for a pause on new data-center projects until protections for electricity supplies, water resources and local communities are in place, with investors fearing similar roadblocks could slow down the AI data center boom once Democratic governors take office in January 2027. The energy investment universe was a mixed bag, with the oil and gas benchmark, State Street Energy Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLE), falling 1.6% to $62.50 on Thursday, as energy stocks tracked the broader market lower despite the rebound in crude. Wednesday’s 8.7% plunge in Brent priced in bets that the election setback would force the Trump administration to pursue a peace deal with Iran and reopen Hormuz. Related: European Gas Prices Drop on Iran Deal Hopes after U.S. Midterms Those bets faded on Thursday , with Eurasia Group cutting its odds of a negotiated agreement to 10% from 20% and putting the likelihood of renewed U.S. strikes at 60%, while Iran’s navy reported that a tanker struck a mine east of the Strait of Hormuz and caught fire. President Trump acknowledged the war’s role in the Republican losses but said the conflict has been worth it. Additionally, Democratic committee chairs are set to deploy their new subpoena powers from January to investigate the administration’s energy dealings. Their targets include its Venezuelan oil concessions to North American Blue Energy Partners, critical mineral deals involving Cantor Fitzgerald, and the cancellation of nearly $8 billion in energy projects in states that voted for Kamala Harris. Separately, two of three Russian tankers carrying diesel to the U.S. under the Trump-Putin deal have abruptly changed course , one toward Brazil and the other into the Mediterranean. “It’s clear there’s hesitancy here in bringing these barrels onshore just because of the implications of doing so,” Kpler analyst Matt Smith said. The Middle East physical oil market has also flipped into a surplus for the first time since July, as crude exports from Arab Gulf producers surged. Combined shipments from Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Iraq and Kuwait rose 10% to 15.53 million barrels per day (bpd) in October, nearing levels recorded at the start of the year. The numbers come from tanker-tracking data compiled by Bloomberg. Saudi Arabia raised exports 13% to 7 million bpd, with shipments from Yanbu on the Red Sea up 35% to 3.07 million bpd. Iraq shipped 3.35 million bpd, up 9.5%, and Kuwait increased exports by a third to 1.44 million bpd. Tanker-tracking data showed no Iranian crude exports for a second month under the U.S. naval blockade. Dubai crude for prompt delivery now trades below later-dated cargoes, a contango structure that means near-term supply exceeds demand. The OPEC Reference Basket, published with a one-day lag, fell 6.4% to $96.87 per barrel in Wednesday’s selloff. Renewable energy stocks gave up their gains after a brief spike on Wednesday

summary: The biggest U.S. shale producers have remained conservative in spending on drilling this year despite the spike in the average WTI crude price by $20 per barrel compared to last year. While signs have emerged that smaller independents have started to take advantage of the higher oil prices to increase drilling, the biggest shale producers are keeping their powder dry amid unprecedented uncertainty in global markets. body: What I Cover Tsvetana Paraskova is an energy and commodities journalist who has contributed to Oilprice.com for nearly a decade, covering global energy markets, commodities,… The biggest U.S. shale producers have remained conservative in spending on drilling this year despite the spike in the average WTI crude price by $20 per barrel compared to last year. While signs have emerged that smaller independents have started to take advantage of the higher oil prices to increase drilling, the biggest shale producers are keeping their powder dry amid unprecedented uncertainty in global markets. One of the top shale producers and the biggest Permian-only focused driller, Diamondback Energy, signaled this week that it will not be splashing on materially increased drilling activity next year as uncertainty remains too high. So far this year, the WTI Crude price has averaged $86.72, more than $20 per barrel compared to the 2025 average of $64.94. The price spike alone is not a reason for loosening capital spending discipline, according to the biggest shale producers, including Diamondback. “I wouldn't say I'm unnecessarily cautious personally, but I think it's always good to prepare the company for a swing to the downside,” Diamondback’s chief executive Kaes Van't Hof told analysts on the Q3 earnings call earlier this week. Diamondback boosted third-quarter earnings, raised its 2026 dividend, and revised up slightly its production outlook for this year, as it generated $2.1 billion in free cash flow for Q3. “Base dividend growth remains a core tenet of the value proposition at Diamondback and our base dividend is now up over 9x since initiating at $0.50 per share in 2018,” Van't Hof wrote in the quarterly letter to shareholders. Diamondback has used excess cash to repurchase bonds and shares and reduce debt in recent months, while it remains cautious about splashing on boosting production. “The macro backdrop is almost exactly as we described last quarter: highly volatile and impossible to predict. The timing of the eventual global oil supply normalization is anyone’s guess, and we therefore expect the current volatility to continue,” Van't Hof told shareholders. “Through this volatility, our priorities remain unchanged: execute with the best capital efficiency in the industry and allocate Free Cash Flow appropriately to maximize long-term stockholder value.” At the earnings call, the executive said he was leaning into the ‘higher-for-longer’ camp of oil price expectations, “but we prepare the business to keep our cost structure low and execution in perfect shape because the inevitable can happen.” Van't Hof noted that “There's just still some uncertainty over the next couple months, and there's just not a need for us to put out a formal 2027 plan because we always end up doing that in February.” The macro picture is so muddied right now that not only Diamondback, but all other U.S. shale producers are unlikely to jump the gun on a significant drilling spree next year just because oil prices are high now. So far this year, U.S. oil production has increased slightly, but not at any scale to offset the massive disruption of supply from the Middle East. The Hormuz crisis has hiked crude oil futures prices and created a shipping crisis with record-high freight rates that raised the actual physical cost of bringing crude oil to refineries. Supermajor ExxonMobil, with its huge Permian position, is not focused on volumes too much, either, despite hitting its production target earlier this year. “We're not real focused, as you know, on necessarily the volume target. It's really around making sure that we're executing it efficiently, deploying the capital efficiently, and then very importantly, leveraging the technology work that we've been doing to maximize the value of that development project,” Exxon’s CEO Darren Woods said on the Q3 earnings call last week. title: Asia Hopes U.S. Midterm Results Will Ease Energy Crisis
summary: Asian countries that depend on oil and gas imports for their energy security are hoping that the results of the U.S. midterms will lead to an end to the war in the Middle East and, consequently, an end to the severe fuel crisis Asian countries are experiencing. The hopes may be premature, however. Trump is still president, and Democrats are no fans of Iran. Asia has been the hardest-hit by the fallout of the U.S. and Israel offensive against Iran that began on February 28. For geographical reasons, the Middle East is the top supplier of hydrocarbons…
body: Asian countries that depend on oil and gas imports for their energy security are hoping that the results of the U.S. midterms will lead to an end to the war in the Middle East and, consequently, an end to the severe fuel crisis Asian countries are experiencing. The hopes may be premature, however. Trump is still president, and Democrats are no fans of Iran. Asia has been the hardest-hit by the fallout of the U.S. and Israel offensive against Iran that began on February 28. For geographical reasons, the Middle East is the top supplier of hydrocarbons to Asia. With that supplier largely gone for an extended period of time, Asian countries were scrambling to secure alternatives—at higher prices. This brought inflation and boosted government spending to try and shield the economy from the worst of the fallout. Last month, the World Bank warned that, essentially, Asia was running out of money because of the energy crisis. “Subsidies have been by far the most common policy response [to the crisis] among emerging and developing economies,” the World Bank said, adding that “Countries with substantial subsidies in place generally have had smaller increases in retail gasoline prices than non-subsidizers, but this relationship weakened considerably for headline inflation.” So, now that Democrats have won a majority in both the House and the Senate, there are hopes they would rein the U.S. president in, including on foreign policy. Reuters’s Clyde Russell wrote in a column this week that the way Democrats can interfere with Trump’s policies is to use congressional power to redirect, cut or boost government spending and to start investigations against Trump himself and close allies and family members. Whether that would be enough to bring down Asian diesel prices remains uncertain. What some observers expect the Democrats to do is ramp up financing for Ukraine at the expense of the Iran war, which will not really change anything with prices because it would simply mean more Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian refineries while Iran remains unconvinced it could make a lasting peace with the United States. Related: European Gas Prices Drop on Iran Deal Hopes after U.S. Midterms This suggests Asian economies are not about to get any fast relief on fuels and other petroleum derivatives, just because the Democrats won 240 seats in the House, versus 147 for the Republicans, and 54 seats in the Senate, versus 44 for the Republicans. In fact, chances are nothing will change much, not fast, anyway. And this means pain at the pump—and everywhere else—will continue. For now, hopes seem to be running high that Democrats will somehow manage to push Trump to make peace with Iran. The details on how exactly remain unclear, but oil prices crashed below $100 on Wednesday following the results of the midterms. This suggests traders are now anticipating an end to the hostilities somehow orchestrated by the Democrat-dominated two houses of parliament. However, some geopolitical analysts have warned that Trump may try to compensate for the election loss at home with an escalation against Iran. Indeed, several analysts from the Middle East have, as cited by Reuters, suggested that an escalation could be Trump’s only option to save face. This does not bode well for Asian economies and, by extension, the rest of the world. Asia was considered the powerhouse of the developing world, the continent where much of the world’s economic growth was taking place and would continue to take place in the coming years. The war has prompted revisions to these forecasts, with fears of recession running high despite delicate phrasing by forecasters. Hopes for a shift in U.S. policies are therefore quite understandable—if possibly misplaced. title: New gold discovery boosts Perpetua’s Stibnite project
summary: Fiddle’s discovery hole returned 109.7 meters grading 3.2 g/t gold and 1.1% antimony, among the most significant mineralized intercepts encountered at the project, the company said.
body: Perpetua Resources (Nasdaq: PPTA) (TSX: PPTA) said it has made a new gold discovery during its 2026 exploration drilling program at its Stibnite Gold project in central Idaho, with over 16,000 meters of core drilling across the project now completed. Perpetua Resources is advancing construction on the $1.3 billion Stibnite Gold project in central Idaho, which was fast-tracked by the Trump administration as part of efforts to strengthen the US critical minerals supply chain. The Stibnite project is set to produce roughly 450,000 ounces of gold annually, supported by proven and probable reserves of 148 million pounds of antimony and more than six million ounces of gold. It is one of the few known US sources of antimony, a mineral essential to defence systems, energy storage, and semiconductors, and one of the largest deposits outside China’s control. Fiddle’s discovery hole, SB633, returned 109.7 meters grading 3.2 g/t gold and 1.1% antimony, among the most significant mineralized intercepts encountered at the project to date, the company said. Located approximately 750 meters south of the permitted Yellow Pine pit along the Meadow Creek Fault Zone, Fiddle adds a new target area to the project’s growing in-pit and near-pit resource base. The north-trending MCFZ is the district’s main ore-controlling structure, which runs through both the Yellow Pine and Hangar Flats deposits and hosts intrusive-hosted mineralization along its flanks. To test the structural controls of the MCFZ, three holes were subsequently drilled, Perpetua said. This included SB637, which extended mineralization to the north and returned 37.4 meters grading 0.7 g/t gold, 0.1% antimony from 93.8 meters downhole. Initial assays from the Fiddle target returned 109.7 meters grading 3.2 g/t gold, 1.1% antimony in hole SB633, beginning at 189 meters downhole. SB633 represents one of the broadest continuous intervals of gold and antimony mineralization returned to date from Stibnite while also exhibiting grades more than double the project’s life-of-mine average. An additional 21 holes were drilled along strike of SB633. Core logging identified both holes as having similar style mineralization to hole SB633, including abundant stibnite and sulfides within the mineralized zones. Follow-up drilling from the Clark Tunnel Fault Zone continued to demonstrate near-surface, high grades including 25.4 meters of 4.5 g/t gold from 13 meters downhole (SB606) and 25.0 meters of 2.3 g/t gold from 18 meters downhole (SB605), the company said. “Given their close proximity to the permitted Yellow Pine pit, Fiddle and the CTFZ were prioritized as key targets for the 2026 exploration program,” Perpetua CEO Jon Cherry said in a news release . “At Fiddle, our initial hole returned broad, continuous mineralization at significant gold and antimony grades which confirm it as an important new discovery. Meanwhile, drilling continues to reinforce the CTFZ as a near-surface, high-grade target on the eastern extent of the Yellow Pine pit,” Cherry said. The RBA is split over the risks of the latest rate hike. For Australians, it’s a bitter pill | Nicki Hutley - The Guardian
body: The country’s economic outlook makes for grim reading – with two major exceptions F inancial markets and economists were of one mind that the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) would this week announce yet another rate hike, its fifth in this cycle, and they did. But it’s probably worth focusing on the fact that three of the nine monetary board members voted to keep rates on hold. To be clear, it’s likely the dissenters agreed that inflation remains too high at present: it clearly is. Underlying inflation, the best indicator of price pressures, has been outside the RBA’s target band (of 2% to 3%) for almost all of the past four years . The dissenters may well have been equally uncomfortable with the increase in inflationary expectations, which jumped up to 5.3% in October. When people expect inflation to be higher, it can allow businesses to more easily pass on price increases – a vicious cycle. Rather, as the governor made clear in her press conference after the decision was announced, the three mavericks felt that the downside risks to the economy from previous rate rises (and likely many other factors) were already large and that yet another increase would risk leaving the Australian economy too weak. The RBA disagrees and thinks the upside risks to inflation are the main game. The press conference showed little nuance, or even respect, for those downside risks. Economics is always about tradeoffs. Since the pandemic, the RBA has tried to stay on its “narrow path”, balancing growth (and employment) goals against inflation targets. With both inflation and unemployment rising, it’s hard to say they are achieving either goal – but hindsight is a wonderful thing. So now our central bankers are telling us there’s to be no more mollycoddling: we will take our medicine until we recover, and it’s bitter medicine indeed. The RBA’s latest forecasts in the accompanying November statement on monetary policy make for some grim reading. Overall economic growth is now expected to slow from 1.6% this financial year to just 1.3% over 2027-28. That implies that growth in per capita GDP (our individual slice of the collective economic pie) will, at best, be flat. Meanwhile, the overall pie only increases as a result of population growth. Along with the slower growth outlook comes higher unemployment, which is expected to hit 5.1% by 2028. This seems to be a rather rosy outlook in my view. Real wages will fall further than previously forecast, as will productivity. Across the economy, the numbers look a lot weaker, with two notable exceptions. The first is, not unexpectedly, public sector demand, which has been left broadly unchanged. No doubt the federal treasurer will continue to face calls to find ways to cut spending (the states are conveniently being overlooked). As an aside, notice it’s automatically assumed that if it’s public sector, it must be “bad” spending, but if it’s private sector, it must be “good”. All that wasteful spending on education, health, our older and less able citizens, not to mention transport. Business investment, on the other hand, gets a free pass, totally unexamined. Business investment is the second area of the forecasts that has been, quite strongly, upgraded – largely the result of datacentre builds. In terms of the economy (as measured by GDP), the datacentres don’t make much of a difference – the imports required to build them count as a negative in our economic accounting system. But datacentres do matter for inflation; the RBA governor even flagged this in her post-meeting conference. The current mantra of proceed at speed on datacentre rollouts comes at a huge cost. Just as the mining boom in the 2000s saw kids ditching education for large wages in the resources sector, this decade our construction workers and tradies – even apprentices – are being enticed to work on datacentres at salaries of multiple what they would get in the residential sector. This not only fuels demand from those workers getting well-a

title: Huge AI stock selloff sends Wall Street reeling as S&P 500 tumbles 4.4% - CommBank
body: A brutal sell-off in AI-linked stocks sent Wall Street sharply lower, with the S&P 500 suffering its worst fall since April 2025 and the Nasdaq tumbling into correction territory. A brutal sell-off swept through Wall Street, led by stocks tied to the buildout of AI data centres. The S&P 500 fell 4.4% on Thursday for its worst drop since President Donald Trump shook markets worldwide in April 2025 with his "Liberation Day" tariffs. The wipeout more than erased the market's gain from the day before , which was its best in three months. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped more than 1,800 points, and the Nasdaq composite tumbled 5.5%. AI stocks worldwide felt pressure as worries rise about possible moratoriums on data centres following Democratic victories in the US midterm elections. US midterms shift the economic outlook: what it could mean for Australia A Democratic sweep of the US midterm elections has changed the balance of power in Washington, but that doesn’t mean things will become more settled, CommBank economists say. The Nasdaq, which is full of AI-related and other tech stocks, sank 11% below its all-time high set last month. A loss of more than 10% off recent highs qualifies as a "correction". Stock markets around the world felt pressure from continued drops for companies that had benefited from the boom in the artificial-intelligence technology industry, and South Korea's Kospi index tumbled 5.3%. Such stocks have been swinging for months on worries that the construction of further AI data centres may slow because of how expensive it's become to borrow money. Critics also said AI stock prices had shot too high and were in a bubble. Tuesday's US midterm elections added another challenge. The nationwide victories by Democrats raised the possibility that governments could force pauses in construction of more data centres. Voters across political parties say they're wary about AI and don't like the increases to power bills caused by data centres. Any slowdown in AI data centre construction would mean fewer purchases of AI chips, not to mention electricity and other products and services that are getting vacuumed up in the AI frenzy, which is driving much of the US economy's growth. Nvidia, the chip company that quickly became the face of the AI boom, fell 8% and was by far the heaviest weight on the S&P 500, a day after dropping 3.2%. Advanced Micro Devices tumbled 14%. CoreWeave, a company that rents access to AI chips to customers over the cloud, fell 8.9%. GE Vernova, which has been helping to power data centres, sank 6.9%. AI chip stocks are some of Wall Street's most influential because they've become some of the largest. A 1% move for Nvidia, for example, has more effect on the S&P 500 than a 1% move for nearly any other US stock. The losses were broad after morning gains for the majority of stocks on Wall Street quickly evaporated. In other financial markets, the initial knee-jerk reaction to the US midterm election results faded a bit. The price of a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 3.9% to $US98.29 and recovered a chunk of its nearly 9% drop from the day before. Uncertainty still reigns about what will happen in the war with Iran and when the global energy industry can return to normal. In the bond market, Treasury yields continued to tumble. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.83% from 4.90% late on Wednesday. It had been at 4.95% on election night and above 5.30% last month. That could be a signal that investors are herding into US Treasury bonds in search of something that's safer to own than stocks. The drop came despite some encouraging reports on the US economy. Fewer US workers applied for unemployment benefits last week. A separate report, meanwhile, suggested overall productivity for US workers improved by more during the northern summer than economists expected. body: Oil Prices Head for 12% Weekly Loss Despite Fresh Tanker Attacks What I Cover Irina Slav has been writing about global energy markets since 2007, covering the oil and gas industry, energy security, commodities, and the… Crude oil prices were on course for a sharp weekly drop, with both Brent crude and WTI shedding 12% since Monday, following the results of the U.S. midterm elections, which gave rise to hopes that the war in the Middle East could be brought to a swift end. At the time of writing, Brent crude was trading at $99.42 per barrel, and West Texas Intermediate was trading at $91.242 per barrel, both up from Thursday’s close on reports of fresh tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz. Reuters reported at least five vessel incidents in the Persian Gulf since Sunday, with threats to commercial traffic persisting despite a recovery in crude shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. The attacks, and skepticism about the prospects of peace between the United States and Iran, despite the Democrats’ victory in the midterms, put a floor under prices. “In the absence of escalation, the oil market is likely to continue to slowly give back the risk premium it built in recent months, with oil flows from the Persian Gulf holding up well,” ING commodity analysts wrote in a note on Thursday. However, the absence of escalation remains only one of two options for President Trump. The other is, indeed, escalation, which would keep prices elevated. “Until there is a credible path to safer, cheaper transit through the Gulf, oil is likely to remain supported on dips and prone to sharp moves on any escalation headlines,” KCM Trade’s chief analyst Tim Waterer said, as quoted by Reuters. Meanwhile, FXPro’s senior market analyst Alex Kuptsikevich noted that “The Republicans’ defeat in the elections does not mean that the conflict in the Middle East will not escalate”, pointing to 2006 and the Iraq war, when Congress also came under the control of Democrats, but this did not change U.S. actions in the Middle East under President George W. title: SanDisk Plunges 22% in a Single Day as AI Data Center Regulatory Risk Swallows Up '378% Revenue Surge' - BigGo Finance
body: SanDisk (SNDK), whose earnings have surged on demand for AI data center storage, was tripped up by a political variable: the outcome of the U.S. midterm elections. On the Nasdaq on Nov. 5 (local time), SanDisk shares closed at $806.43, down 22.26% from the prior session. That decline stands out against Micron's 17.16% drop and Western Digital's 17.39% slide the same day. With the Nasdaq Composite down about 5.5%, the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) fell more than 11%, its worst day since March 2020. The trigger for the selloff was politics, not earnings. With Democrats winning both the Senate and the House and also prevailing in key gubernatorial races, fears have grown over tighter regulation of AI data center construction. The calculation that expansion schedules could be delayed by power and water procurement and permitting issues—pushing back orders for NAND Flash and SSDs—stripped buying interest from the sector broadly. The earnings themselves beat market expectations. SanDisk's fiscal 2027 first-quarter revenue, disclosed on Oct. 29, came in at $11.031 billion, up 378% year over year and 23% quarter over quarter. Data center revenue was $4.802 billion, up 61% from the prior quarter and accounting for about 44% of total revenue. Adjusted earnings per share (EPS) improved to $49.51 from $39.25 in the prior quarter. According to the company, about 60% of the quarter-over-quarter revenue increase came from higher volume and 40% from higher prices. Guidance for the next quarter also assumes continued growth. The company projected revenue of $12.2 billion to $12.6 billion and adjusted EPS of $55 to $57. Consumer business revenue, however, fell 29% quarter over quarter to $397 million, revealing a phase in which the market is adjusting to higher prices. CEO David Goeckeler said at the time of the earnings release, "We started fiscal 2027 with another strong quarter, and as product demand grew solidly, our data center business drove faster growth." The problem is valuation. SanDisk shares had climbed more than 450% year to date through Oct. 29, and the recent plunge has pulled them about 65% off their peak of $2,354. Even so, the year-to-date gain still exceeds 250%. After such a run-up, the stock is structurally vulnerable to any single signal of slowing AI investment or a peak in memory prices. RBC Capital cut its price target to $1,400 from $1,600 the day after the earnings release and maintained its "Sector Perform" rating. The revision reflected a decline in valuation multiples across the memory sector, even though results and guidance exceeded expectations. The episode illustrates the volatility of the entire AI infrastructure investment cycle rather than a problem specific to SanDisk. Given that earnings surged on the combination of strong NAND prices and data center expansion, the key variable for the stock's direction going forward is whether customer orders and long-term supply contracts are carried out as scheduled even if the policy environment changes. The fact that the semiconductor sector broadly saw a double-digit correction in a single day also suggests that regulatory risk is not confined to any one stock.

title: Vertiv's Push Beyond the Data Center Runs Into a Political Reality Check - ad-hoc-news.de
body: Vertiv is widening its commercial reach at the very moment investors are questioning how fast the world will actually build the facilities that anchor its business. Gustavo Pérez laid out plans to extend the company's mission-critical infrastructure work into industrial, healthcare and transportation applications in Latin America — a diversification pitch that landed alongside a 14% one-day slide in the stock as political anxiety swept through AI and data center names. The two developments tell different stories. One is about where Vertiv wants to be in five years. The other is about what the market is willing to pay for that ambition today. The case for moving beyond data centers is straightforward. Roughly 85% of Vertiv's expected worldwide revenue for 2026 is projected to come from data centers, according to Mexico Business News. That concentration is precisely what makes adjacent markets interesting to shareholders, and also what limits how much they can move the needle. Their economic weight will determine whether the expansion genuinely broadens the company or merely decorates the pitch. In industrial settings, Vertiv is targeting uninterruptible power supplies and batteries for critical loads rather than blanket protection for an entire factory. It is a focused approach that makes sense if customers are willing to pay for extra assurance on their most important processes — a specific need addressed with a specific product, rather than an all-encompassing safety net. Healthcare and transportation round out the list of expansion fields Pérez described. Each offers additional development runway, but only becomes meaningful as a counterweight to the data center concentration once it contributes a correspondingly larger share of revenue. Mexico offers the most concrete foothold. Vertiv runs four manufacturing sites and an operations center in Querétaro, and Pérez expects Mexican projects to grow in 2027. He was equally direct about the precondition: the country must accelerate its energy infrastructure build-out to attract investment in AI data centers. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying Vertiv? Querétaro and the Bajío region are already industry hubs, according to Pérez. Vertiv's collaboration with Nvidia on power supply and liquid cooling for graphics processors adds a technological dimension to that local presence — support that holds up as long as customers can actually bring their planned facilities to life. The Mexican story captures both sides of the equation: industrial footprint and relevant engineering on one hand, dependence on power capacity and project execution on the other. Vertiv has been busy on the deal front as well. It closed the acquisition of UtilityInnovation Group on October 27, paying approximately $1.45 billion in cash upfront, with up to $1.15 billion in additional contingent cash consideration tied to conditions. That distinction matters: the initial payment is done, while the earn-out remains contingent. Investors evaluating the deal should neither treat the conditional amount as already spent nor ignore it — the obligation belongs to the expansion story just as much as the revenue opportunity does. A day earlier, on October 26, Vertiv completed its purchase of King Environmental Services, which the company says extends services around fluid management, commissioning and load testing across Europe, the Middle East and Africa. The same day brought the launch of SmartIT, a prefabricated infrastructure solution combining rack infrastructure with power conversion and distribution, liquid cooling and monitoring, aimed at enterprise and data center deployments. The pattern is clear: Vertiv is moving from selling components to selling integrated systems and the services that surround them.
